I have farmed this land for thirty years, since I was twenty years old. My body knows the rhythm of the seasons better than any book. With 6.5 mu and two family members working off-farm in the city, I cannot spread myself too thin—cotton brings good money but it is a labor devil that demands hand-picking and endless spraying. So this year, like last year, I will keep 5 mu in my wheat-maize rotation. That is my foundation. The wheat goes in after autumn harvest with an improved variety from the county supply station; I rotary till after the maize comes off, spread the base fertilizer, and then irrigate three times from my well: the freezing water before winter, the jointing water in spring, and one more when the heads are filling. At jointing I top-dress urea—my eyes can tell when the wheat is hungry. As soon as the wheat is threshed in early June, I sow hybrid maize directly into the stubble without plowing. There is no time to waste between crops, and leaving the ground untouched holds the moisture. Maize is simpler: two irrigations, usually at the big trumpet stage and grain filling, and two pesticide passes if the armyworms stay away. The remaining 1.5 mu I plant cotton because a household needs cash for school fees and medicine. Cotton must be ploughed properly to warm the soil, and I will spray four times because the bollworm never sleeps. I know my soil, and I know my strength. I do not gamble.
